tool_args.old_string: Multi-turn dialogue with LLMs suffers from progressive attention decay toward system-prompt goal tokens. On Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, the Goal Accessibility Ratio (GAR) declines 70.8\% between early and mid-conversation turns, yet linear probes recover goal content from the residual stream (AUC\,=\,0.98). We introduce ThreadGate, per-layer content-and-turn-conditioned MLP gates trained jointly with next-token prediction and an auxiliary GAR loss. A five-way controlled comparison shows training succeeds (teacher-forced GAR\,=\,0.50) but autoregressive GAR collapses to 0.019--0.064, an 8--17$\times$ gap; turn-conditioned gating significantly outperforms LoRA-only ($p$\,=\,0.004) but the residual gap remains large (7.8$\times$), and PCGrad excludes gradient conflict. The failure traces to exposure bias: attention patterns learned under teacher-forced prefixes do not transfer to model-generated text. Steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR to 0.727 and scheduled sampling compresses the gap to 1.44$\times$ (single seed); cross-model evaluation on Llama-3.1-8B confirms the gap (27$\times$ by median). These findings characterize how exposure bias selectively destroys auxiliary attention losses while leaving the primary NTP objective robust.
tool_args.new_string: Fine-tuned to allocate 50\% of attention to system-prompt goals (GAR\,=\,0.50 under teacher forcing), Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct retains only GAR\,=\,0.064 under autoregressive generation---an 8$\times$ collapse. We trace this failure to exposure bias: attention patterns optimized under teacher-forced prefixes do not transfer to model-generated text. ThreadGate, per-layer content-and-turn-conditioned MLP gates trained with an auxiliary GAR loss, provides a controlled testbed. A five-way comparison isolates turn conditioning, gating, gradient conflict, and fine-tuning; each pair kills one hypothesis. Gating outperforms LoRA-only ($p$\,=\,0.004) but the gap remains 7.8$\times$; PCGrad eliminates gradient conflict but \emph{worsens} AR GAR ($p$\,=\,0.002), ruling out the most intuitive failure mechanism by \emph{modus tollens}. Steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR to 0.727; scheduled sampling compresses the gap to 1.44$\times$ (single seed). Cross-model evaluation on Llama-3.1-8B confirms a 27$\times$ gap. These findings establish that exposure bias selectively destroys auxiliary attention losses while NTP self-recovers---a failure mode with no prior multi-turn transformer characterization.

\paragraph{Exposure bias.}
Teacher forcing creates a distributional mismatch between training and inference that compounds over sequence length \citep{wiseman2016sequence,arora2022exposure}. Scheduled Sampling \citep{bengio2015scheduled} introduced curriculum-based mixing of ground-truth and model-generated tokens. MIXER \citep{ranzato2016sequence} combined token-level and sequence-level objectives, and Professor Forcing \citep{lamb2016professor} used adversarial regularization to align hidden state distributions under both regimes. \citet{he2019exposure} showed that autoregressive models exhibit self-recovery from exposure bias at the token prediction level. SEARNN \citep{leblond2018searnn} proposed locally recurrent search-based training to avoid the mismatch entirely. This literature focuses on primary objective degradation in single-turn or sequence-to-sequence settings. Two gaps remain: no work examines how exposure bias affects \emph{auxiliary} objectives targeting attention distributions, and no multi-turn transformer equivalent of these classical RNN-era mitigations exists. Our work fills both gaps: we identify a distinct failure mode where auxiliary attention losses converge under teacher forcing but collapse under autoregressive generation (8--27$\times$), and we provide the first evidence that scheduled sampling transfers to multi-turn transformer attention objectives.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The failure traces to an incompatibility between teacher-forcing and GAR-family auxiliary losses, not to the gating architecture. NTP gradient pressure (7.5--14.7$\times$ the GAR magnitude) pushes gates toward identity (2--7\% attenuation). Inference-time steering ($\beta$\,=\,5) recovers GAR from 0.064 to 0.727, providing constructive evidence that attention misallocation is a proximal cause (\S\ref{subsec:steering}).

\paragraph{Scheduled sampling confirms exposure bias.} Scheduled sampling \citep{bengio2015scheduled} mixes teacher-forced and model-generated contexts during training, increasing AR GAR-ours from 0.064 to 0.347 (5.4$\times$) and compressing the 7.8$\times$ gap to 1.44$\times$ with negligible PPL change (1.44 vs.\ 1.43); a second seed yields 0.418 (gap 1.20$\times$). By directly targeting the train-inference mismatch, this implicates exposure bias as the dominant factor; the gating benefit diminishes in longer dialogues (Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-n5}), consistent with compounding over turns.

\paragraph{Downstream effects.} KV cache drift---model-generated key-value states diverging from teacher-forced statistics---is a downstream consequence of exposure bias rather than an independent cause; disentangling requires a switching experiment (future work).
